For **PostgreSQL**, ``delete retain`` and ``delete before`` order backups using the timeline and WAL segment embedded in each backup name by default. Pass the global flag ``--use-sentinel-time`` on ``delete`` to order by backup start time from sentinel/metadata when it is available; see PostgreSQL.md.

Cratis Chronicle is an open-source (MIT) event-sourcing database and runtime for applications that need a history of meaningful changes. Record application changes as events, build queryable views with declarative projections, and react to events from .NET, TypeScript, Kotlin/Java, or Elixir.

Chronicle's declarative projections map events onto **read models**, views shaped for the queries your application serves. The kernel handles processing and storage updates. **Reactors** run your code when events arrive, for example to send a notification. Materialized views update after the append, so choose the consistency behavior your workflow needs.

For personal data, Chronicle encrypts fields marked as **personally identifiable information (PII)** under a subject's key and supports erasing that key without removing the event's position in the log. These mechanisms support your compliance work; they do not make an application compliant by themselves. Read Compliance before recording personal data.

The Orleans-based .NET kernel has a first-class .NET SDK and additional TypeScript, Kotlin/Java (JVM), and Elixir clients; a Python client is coming soon. Storage providers include MongoDB (default), PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite, and in-memory implementations. Client and provider capabilities differ, so use the guide for your chosen setup. Chronicle and its bundled web workbench run without Studio, Arc, or Components. Chronicle is free to use and MIT licensed; free AI skills are also available for working with the code and documentation.
- ⚙️ **Chronicle Kernel** — the server that manages event storage, processing, and querying, built on Microsoft Orleans for distributed, stateful processing
- 🌍 **Language-agnostic gRPC contracts** — protobuf contracts that any language can implement, with clients for TypeScript, Kotlin/Java, and Elixir, and a Python client coming soon
- ⌨️ **CLI** — the Cratis CLI brings event, observer, projection, and read-model inspection to the terminal

**What this can and cannot verify, honestly:** `BACKUPDRILL_SANDBOX_URL` connects as the sandbox **superuser**, and superusers bypass row-level security. The sandbox does carry a stub of the Supabase runtime — an `auth` schema whose `uid()`/`jwt()`/`role()`/`email()` return null, and the `anon`/`authenticated`/`service_role` roles — so functions, column defaults and policies that reference them restore instead of being skipped. The sandbox deliberately does not create Supabase-managed *tables* such as `auth.users`: an index, constraint or policy that points at one is reported as a skipped managed object (these are restored in a second, post-data pass where that exemption applies). A skipped foreign key into `auth.users` still matters for a real restore, see Tables that reference auth.users. A *view* over one is created in the strict first pass instead, and fails the drill — a real gap in what a public-only backup can rebuild, shown rather than hidden. A function *body* that selects from `auth.users` is different: PostgreSQL does not validate string-literal bodies (`AS $$ … $$`) during a restore (`check_function_bodies` is off in every dump), so such a function is recreated and the drill passes — it would only fail when called. The exception is an SQL-standard `BEGIN ATOMIC … END` body, which is parsed and dependency-checked at creation regardless of that setting, so one of those referencing a managed table fails the drill like a view does. That is exactly what `--check-cmd` is for: if your application depends on such a function, call it there. So use `--check-cmd` for data and business invariants ("orders reference existing users", "the row count I care about is sane"). It is **not** an RLS behavior test — `auth.uid()` is a stub and you are a superuser; verifying RLS takes an authenticated client stack with real JWTs, which no restore sandbox can fake generically.

`--dry-run` writes nothing to the target. Besides checking the target (not the source project, schemas empty, Postgres and `pg_restore` versions, extensions available), it downloads the dump to a temporary directory, checks its sha256 and looks for foreign keys that point outside the backup (see Tables that reference auth.users). The real run repeats those checks before it writes anything; a foreign key into a table that one of the recorded extensions creates is checked again once the extensions are installed. The database restore then runs in a single transaction: if any statement fails, nothing from the snapshot stays on the target, and you can run it again on the same project once you've fixed the cause. (If the connection drops while it commits, the error says so and asks you to check the target first.) Right after that transaction commits, the grants for `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` are set in a transaction of their own (see Grants for anon, authenticated and service_role). Foreign keys between two tables in the backup are the exception to the single transaction: they're added after that, in one more. If rows in your data already break one of them (deleting with triggers switched off, for example under `session_replication_role = replica`, can leave rows like that), the key is added as `NOT VALID` instead of failing the restore. Those rows come back as they are, new writes are still checked, and the report names the key and, when it can count them, how many rows break it. Keys on or into partitioned tables, keys into an extension's tables, and every key in an archive whose foreign key statements BackupDrill can't fully read stay in the main transaction, so a broken one rolls the whole restore back. A key over a generated column is added in the second step but is never relaxed, because the restore recomputes those values; if it breaks, that step fails. Keys added as `NOT VALID` don't fail a drill: the drill passes and lists them in its report. If a step after the main transaction fails for any other reason, the tables and data are already on the target and the error says so. Extensions the run installed stay installed, since the next run needs them too, and the empty-target check doesn't count objects that belong to an extension (except an extension's configuration tables, whose rows a dump can carry). One transaction holds a lock on every table, index and sequence until it commits, so a very large schema can run out of lock slots: on Supabase's smallest compute size, about a thousand tables (partitions count as tables). The restore then stops with nothing written and tells you how to raise `max_locks_per_transaction`.

One error is expected and harmless: `schema "public" already exists` — the target always has it. An error on a foreign key into `auth.users` means the users have to be copied in first (see Tables that reference auth.users). After that, set the grants yourself (next section). Don't use `--clean` against a Supabase project: it drops and recreates the `public` schema, and with it the grants Supabase put on it. The `backupdrill restore` command above handles all of this (plus verification) for you.

The dump doesn't carry grants, so a restored table only gets what the target project hands out by default. Supabase used to grant every new table in `public` to all three roles. It stopped doing that for new projects on May 30, 2026, and for existing projects on October 30, 2026 (Supabase's announcement). On a project that has switched, a plain `pg_restore` brings back every table and row, and the app still gets `42501` on all of them. On a project that hasn't switched yet, it does the opposite: every restored table is open to `anon`, including the ones you had closed.

- **Many writers stop waiting on each other.** When goroutines write at the same time, the driver runs their autocommit `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` statements as one transaction and commits once. Each call still gets its own error, `LastInsertId` and `RowsAffected`, and returns only after the commit, so nothing is less durable. When one statement fails so badly that SQLite rolls back the whole transaction (an IO error, `ON CONFLICT ROLLBACK`, a context that ends while it runs), the statements merged before it fail with `ABORT_ROLLBACK`, and none runs twice.
